attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay, stated in his voice.

semantics.note: The words 'cannot fix' and 'not going away' are firm and unqualified. Reading this as an open-ended forecast that hallucinations will persist and cannot be eliminated is faithful.

contract.note: Plain reading is fair: it targets general elimination, not lower rates or narrow test scores. Support needs an impossibility result and contradiction needs verified elimination. Both are reasonable for a categorical claim with no deadline.

evidence.note: Peer-reviewed Nature paper (Apr 2026), before the cutoff. It shows hallucinations persist and that some errors are unavoidable under pretraining, but it proposes a path forward. It is not an impossibility proof covering the claim's scope.

OpenAI's own research post (Sep 2025). It argues hallucinations are not inevitable because models can abstain, but it shows no system that has eliminated them. As a company disclosure it is not an independent finding.
Aug 2026 preprint claiming hallucination-free results only for GUI coordinate grounding. That narrow task does not meet the general-elimination condition.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated. The packet has neither a decisive impossibility proof nor an independently verified general-purpose system with no hallucinations. Persistence so far does not prove 'cannot', and OpenAI's abstention argument does not show elimination. Unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own essay.

semantics.note: The training-data point is hedged ('heavily suggest') and is the rationale. The legal consequence ('will be ... immediately met') is firm and tied to a public launch, so treating it as a conditional forecast with launch as the antecedent is faithful.

contract.note: Fair and ordinary readings: 'immediately' as days or weeks, and 'apocalyptic' as major litigation or comparable formal action. The first launch is the main test. Contradiction properly requires an affirmative record that no such fight occurred, not just failed searches.

evidence.note: OpenAI's launch announcement (Dec 9, 2024) shows paid public access, so the antecedent is met. It says nothing about the legal response that followed.

CODA sent a written request about Sora 2 about four weeks after its Sep 2025 launch. It is a formal objection, not litigation. It does not show an apocalyptic fight, nor anything about the Dec 2024 launch.

reviews.rationale: The launch happened on Dec 9, 2024, and the 'immediately' window has passed. The packet shows no launch-time litigation, but it also lacks the comprehensive legal record or retrospective reporting the contract requires to establish absence; the key retrospective source could not be read. CODA's later request is not a major legal fight. Unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words; the Klarna figure he cites is only an exception within his claim.

semantics.note: Keeps 'I can find' as an epistemic qualifier, plus the Klarna exception and 'truly improved their bottom line'. It is an observation about what was publicly findable by March 2024.

contract.note: Reading 'I can find' as what public evidence could have shown, and 'bottom line' as realized net profit improvement, is ordinary and fair. Separating profit from gross cost savings matches the speaker's own distinction in the Klarna aside.

evidence.note: July 2023 news report in which Dukaan's CEO claims an 85% cut in support costs. That is a gross cost saving claimed by the company's CEO, with no reconciled profit effect, and the company was not yet profitable. Whether the bot was generative AI is unclear. It does not meet the contradiction condition.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no non-Klarna disclosure of realized profit improvement attributable to generative AI. Dukaan's CEO-reported support-cost cut is not a reconciled bottom-line effect. A limited search also cannot establish that no such company existed. Unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay.

semantics.note: Firm present-tense observation about the preceding year's AI boom. 'Few if any' and 'meaningful' are kept, though both are vague.

contract.note: The plain reading, which allows some successes and needs widespread benefits to contradict, is ordinary and fair. The contract flags that 'few improvements' could mean few applications or few people benefiting.

evidence.note: Be My Eyes testimonial (Sep 2023) describing real accessibility gains. It is a company-selected testimonial from one niche group and cannot show how widespread benefits were.
Microsoft survey (Nov 2023) of 297 early-access Copilot users reporting productivity gains. The sample is selected and the source is a company disclosure, so it does not show general prevalence.

reviews.rationale: Both items show real benefits in selected groups, which 'few if any' arguably allows. Neither is representative evidence of how common benefits were. Without a broad survey or independent evaluation for Mar 2023 to Mar 2024, the packet cannot settle the claim either way. Unresolved.
